title: Be still (Psalm 46:10)
hook: be still, and know that I am God

segments.voice: Yesterday: the quiet time, a notebook and a mug before the day begins. Your line was first thing, a little quiet. Did the quiet get the first word this morning? Day one hundred forty-five.

You've probably seen these words somewhere. On a mug. A throw pillow. A calm lake photo on someone's wall, with a single line in soft script: be still, and know that I am God. It looks like a spa brochure. Gentle, peaceful, a little sleepy. So here's the surprise. The psalm that line comes from doesn't picture a quiet lake. It pictures the ground giving way, and a war. Mountains sliding into the sea. Nations raging. Kingdoms toppling. Bows, spears and chariots. And right in the middle of all that noise, God speaks two words. Today, be still, and why it's much stronger than it looks on the pillow.
screen: `ON A MUG, BY A CALM LAKE.` → `BUT THE PSALM IS LOUD.` → `EARTHQUAKE AND WAR.`

segments.voice: Be still. Psalm forty-six opens like this, in the King James Bible: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." Then it gets loud. "Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea." The waters roar, the nations rage, kingdoms are moved, the earth melts. Then the psalm turns: God "maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder." And only then, verse ten: "Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth." Now the Hebrew. Be still is one word, harpu. Its root means to let go, to sink down, to let your hands drop. Like soldiers told to lower their weapons. Like someone who's been gripping the wheel for hours finally unclenching. So it's less relax, more stop. Drop it. Let go. Some scholars think it's spoken first to the warring nations: stop fighting, and know who's God. Others hear it spoken to the frightened people inside the city. Plenty of readers hear both. Either way, stillness here is not calm scenery. It's what happens when you stop trying to hold up the mountains yourself. Martin Luther loved this psalm; his great hymn A Mighty Fortress Is Our God grew out of it. And Jews and Christians alike have prayed it in wartime, in plague and in grief. The pillow isn't wrong. It's just missing the earthquake. The stillness is meant for the moment everything is shaking.
screen: `A VERY PRESENT HELP IN TROUBLE.` · `MOUNTAINS INTO THE SEA.` · `HARPU — LET GO, DROP YOUR HANDS.` · `STILLNESS IN THE EARTHQUAKE.` · then, large: `BE STILL, AND KNOW THAT I AM GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Two minutes of stillness. Sit, and let your hands rest open on your knees or in your lap. Notice where you're gripping: your jaw, your shoulders, your hands. Let each one drop, the way the Hebrew word suggests. Think of the thing that's shaking in your life right now. Don't solve it. Just let go of holding it up for two minutes. If you pray, you can say the line slowly, once: be still, and know that I am God. Then stay still. If you don't pray, just stay. The bell holds the time.
Be still. In Hebrew, harpu: let go, drop your hands. Said in the middle of an earthquake and a war.
Your line: be still, and know. Today, when something shakes you, drop your hands for three breaths before you grab for it. Day one hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 46 in times of fear or crisis, and some use 'be still, and know that I am God' as a short prayer in silent or contemplative prayer, repeated slowly with the breath.

original.note: Hebrew: let go, relax your grip, let your hands drop — rendered be still.

trapdoor: what you thought: be still means relax, a nice line for a pillow.
what it means: stop, let go, drop your hands, spoken in the middle of an earthquake and a war.
what a scholar hears: harpu, from the root r-f-h, to sink or slacken. some hear it as a command to warring nations: cease fighting.

notes: Hebrew harpu (הַרְפּוּ), hiphil imperative of r-f-h, to sink, relax, let drop. Confirm vocalization and gloss.
Addressees of 46:10 (warring nations vs. God's people): both readings presented without ranking. Confirm.
Luther's Ein feste Burg (c. 1527–1529) based on Psalm 46: confirm.
'Jews and Christians alike have prayed it in wartime, in plague and in grief': general claim; confirm.

Audit (second sample): the hook said the psalm is 'set in' an earthquake and a war with 'spears and chariots everywhere'; the psalm only imagines the earth giving way ('though the earth be removed'), and its spears and chariots are the ones God breaks and burns. Now 'it pictures the ground giving way, and a war', with the myth reveal to match. 'Most Christians hear both' (unsourced) is now 'plenty of readers hear both'.
